source.title: Applicability of scaling laws to vision encoding models
source.authors: Takuya Matsuyama; K. Sasaki; Shinji Nishimoto

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling in vision-based brain-encoding models, a new setting, using downstream prediction accuracy rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling of brain-encoding prediction accuracy with fMRI training-sample size and vision-model parameter size. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, extrapolation from fitted small runs, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture effects at a fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: The study varies vision-model parameter size (EVA-02-CLIP base/large/enormous and four other models) and reports how a downstream task, fMRI brain-encoding accuracy from frozen features, changes. That bears on V6 in a new setting. The fMRI sample-size sweep scales the ridge readout's training data, not the pretrained model, so it does not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that accuracy scales approximately log-linearly with fMRI sample size across lower to higher visual regions. They find log-linear scaling with vision-model parameter size, especially in higher visual areas. The parameter-size claim rests on the EVA-02-CLIP series only; across all models the trend was not log-linear.
record.recipe_differences: Uses voxel-wise ridge-regression brain-encoding models and measures validation prediction accuracy, rather than language-model held-out pretraining loss; no compute-optimal split or extrapolation fit is evaluated.
record.method_sensitivity: The parameter-size trend differs between the EVA-02-CLIP series and the comparison across all vision models; the reported trend is especially apparent in higher-order visual fields. The authors point to architecture, training methods, and training-data quality as additional factors.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain-encoding accuracy improves approximately log-linearly with the number of fMRI samples used to fit the ridge-regression readout, across ROIs (Section 3.1, Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain-encoding model accuracy scales log-linearly with the encoding-model training-set size.

record.problems: Parameter-size results are reported as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The cross-model comparison varies architecture, training modality, and training details as well as parameter count, so it does not isolate parameter count across all models.

untested.parts: Whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss. Whether fitted trends extrapolate. Language-model downstream tasks. Any quantitative fit of accuracy versus parameters.

record.verdict_notes: This is a short Algonauts challenge report. All scaling results are figure-only, with no fitted exponents, numbers or uncertainty. The abstract says 4.3B while Table 1 says 4.4B for EVA-02-CLIP-enormous. Linking to V6 assumes brain encoding from frozen features counts as a downstream task for vision models; reviewers may judge this outside the claim's language-model scope.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Architecture effects controlled at a fixed parameter count.
The study tests visual brain-encoding prediction accuracy, not whether held-out pretraining loss has the same power-law form across modalities or training regimes.
The study examines brain-encoding prediction accuracy, not a range of other downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup, and bending of pretraining-loss curves.

rows.subject: EVA-02-CLIP-large
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of fMRI samples used to train voxel-wise encoding models.

conditions.value: seven ROIs; prediction accuracy averaged across ROIs is also plotted
features from each layer of EVA-02-CLIP-large

rows.note: The authors state that accuracy improved approximately log-linearly as training samples increased. The plotted result is aggregated across subjects; the text says the trend held across the ROIs.
rows.check: This row varies the number of fMRI samples used to fit the linear ridge encoding model with fixed EVA-02-CLIP-large features. It does not scale the pretrained model's parameters, tokens or compute, so it measures a different construct. It is moved to fits_no_version. The record says the plotted result is averaged across subjects. The text says it is averaged across subjects per ROI, with an ROI average curve.

rows.subject: all vision models compared
rows.size_stated: 86M to 4.4B parameters, as stated in the abstract and Table 1
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoding-model prediction accuracy across vision models with different parameter counts.

conditions.value: each ROI; results averaged across subjects

rows.note: Aggregate comparison across models. The authors say accuracy did not appear to scale log-linearly across all models; they also note architecture, training methods, and training-data quality as relevant factors.
rows.check: Figure only. The models differ in architecture (CNN vs Transformer), training modality and data as well as size, so parameter count is confounded. Authors say accuracy across all models 'does not appear to scale log-linearly'.

rows.subject: EVA-02-CLIP series
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoding-model prediction accuracy across EVA-02-CLIP models of different parameter counts.

conditions.value: ventral, lateral, and parietal higher-order visual fields

rows.note: Aggregate result for the EVA-02-CLIP series. The authors say the series appears to scale log-linearly, especially in higher-order visual fields.
rows.check: Figure only, with three model sizes, no fitted law and no uncertainty. The authors' wording is hedged ('appears to scale log-linearly').

rows.subject: EVA-02-CLIP series
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoding-model prediction accuracy across EVA-02-CLIP models of different parameter counts.

conditions.value: all ROIs, including lower-order visual fields

rows.note: The authors say the EVA-02-CLIP series appears to scale log-linearly, with the pattern especially evident in higher-order fields; no separate trend is stated for each lower-order field.
rows.check: The text gives no separate statement for lower-order fields. Partial is inferred from the trend being 'especially' evident in higher-order fields, and is weakly grounded.

relationships.condition: EVA-02-CLIP series (0.086B, 0.3B, 4.4B), higher-order visual ROIs (ventral, lateral, parietal), 4500 training samples
relationships.reason: Encoding accuracy appears to rise log-linearly with parameter count within one model family (R3); figure only, three points.
relationships.display_finding: Encoding accuracy appeared to increase log-linearly with parameter count across three model sizes.

relationships.condition: Comparison across all six vision models of differing architecture and training modality; lower-order visual ROIs
relationships.reason: Across model families accuracy does not appear log-linear in parameters, and the trend is weaker outside higher-order fields (R2, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy did not appear log-linear in parameters across model families, and scaling trends were weaker outside higher-order visual fields.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
